9.1 · Earth's Internal Structure

From Core to Crust

Core
Iron and nickel. Solid inner core; liquid outer core. Convection of the liquid iron, organized by Earth's rotation, generates the magnetic field.
Mantle
84% of Earth's volume; mostly solid rock that creeps slowly over geologic time.
Crust
Thin, brittle outermost layer. The solid surface we live on.
Magnetosphere
The magnetic field shields Earth from charged solar particles and guides animal migration.
Litho- / Asthenosphere
Rigid lithosphere (crust + upper mantle, ~60–90 mi) rides on the pliable asthenosphere.
9.1 · Migration, Magnetic Fields & Monarch Butterflies

Navigating by Earth's Magnetic Field

  • Churning liquid iron in Earth's outer core, organized by the planet's rotation, generates a magnetic field, the same field that moves a compass needle and helps animals find their way.
  • Monarch butterflies use magnetic sensors in their antennae to migrate from Canada and the US to Mexico each fall, returning north in spring and summer.
  • Many other animals navigate the same way: rainbow trout, the Arctic tern, and sea turtles all rely on the magnetic field.

Route after USDA Forest Service, “Monarch Butterfly Migration and Overwintering” (fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/pollinators/Monarch_Butterfly/migration)

9.2 · How Does Earth Recycle and Renew Its Surface?

The Rock Cycle

Igneous Rock
Formed when magma cools and crystallizes. Hawaii's lava flows create new land as they solidify.
Uplift, Weathering & Erosion
Uplift raises buried rock to the surface; wind, water, ice, and gravity then break it down and carry it away. Human farming accelerated the 1930s Dust Bowl.
Sedimentary Rock
Sediment is buried in layers and lithified under pressure into solid rock.
Metamorphic Rock
Deep burial transforms existing rock with heat and pressure. Enough heat melts any rock back into magma, and the cycle can run in any direction.

9.3 · Why Are Minerals Important, and How Do We Get Them?

Rare Earth Elements

  • Minerals from Earth's crust are essential for electronics, solar panels, wind turbines, and electric vehicles. Most rare earth metals come from China.
  • Global dependence: rare earth “supply” is geographically concentrated, creating strategic vulnerabilities.
  • Environmental cost: produces radioactive mill tailings, toxic ponds, and waste sludge (causing crop death and community illness).
  • Implication: the 'clean energy' transition requires mining that carries its own environmental justice concerns.
  • Sustainability strategy: recycle and reuse rare earth minerals from consumer electronics to reduce extraction demand.

9.4 · What Shapes Earth's Surface?

Landscapes, Landforms & Watersheds

  • A landscape is built from landforms (its surface features) and topography (the shape of the land).
  • A watershed is the area of land draining to a point along a river (the Mississippi drains 31 states and 2 Canadian provinces).
  • Floodplains slow rivers and let sediment settle; a delta is a landform formed by the deposition of sediments at a river's mouth.

9.5 · What Is Soil, and Where Does It Come From?

Soil Formation & Structure

Soil: a complex mixture of weathered rock, mineral particles, decaying organic matter, water, air, and living organisms. Formed where the lithosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere meet.

O Horizon (Organic)
When present, a surface layer of decomposing plant and animal matter; nutrient-rich.
A Horizon (Topsoil)
Complex mix of minerals and organic matter. Most biologically active layer.
B Horizon (Subsoil)
Mineral matter leached from above. Less organic content.
C Horizon (Parent Material)
Weathered bedrock or sediment. Foundation for soil development above.

Sustainability: Healthy soil supports plant growth and nutrient cycling.

Where Soil Was Pushed Too Far

Tap a place. Make your guess. Then watch what happened.

Pick a numbered place on the map.

1California Deltasince the 1850s

A peat marsh was drained and plowed.

How far below sea level are many central Delta islands now?

10 to nearly 25 feet below sea level

Drained peat rots into carbon dioxide, 1 to 3 inches a year. More than 1,100 miles of levees hold the rivers back.

USGS Fact Sheet 005-00, Delta Subsidence in California (2000)

2Great Plains1930s

Prairie was plowed for wheat, then drought hit.

On May 11, 1934, how far did one storm carry Plains soil?

Over Washington, D.C. and far out into the Atlantic

In March 1935 dust darkened Washington again as Congress held hearings. Weeks later it created the Soil Conservation Service.

USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, A Brief History of NRCS

3Corn Beltsince the 1800s

Generations of plowing on rolling hills.

How much of the Corn Belt has lost all of its dark, carbon-rich topsoil?

About one-third of the Corn Belt

Hilltops are down to pale subsoil. Crop yields there run about 6% lower.

Thaler, Larsen & Yu (2021), PNAS 118(8)

4Mesopotamia3500 to 1700 BC

Fields were irrigated for centuries. The water left its salt behind.

Around 3500 BC farmers grew half wheat, half barley. By 1700 BC, how much wheat?

None: wheat could no longer grow

Salt-tolerant barley took over: 80% of the crop by 2500 BC, all of it by 1700 BC.

USGS Fact Sheet 170-98 (1998), after Jacobsen & Adams (1958), Science

5Chinasurvey 2005 to 2013

Factories, mines and farm chemicals reached the fields.

What share of China’s farmland soil samples were contaminated beyond the national standard?

About 1 in 5 (19.4%)

Cadmium, nickel and arsenic topped the list.

China’s Ministry of Environmental Protection and Ministry of Land and Resources, National Soil Contamination Survey (2014)

6Western Australiasince the 1900s

Deep-rooted bush was cleared for wheat and sheep.

How much farmland in the southwest has turned salty?

1 to 2 million hectares

Without deep roots, salty groundwater rose to the surface. The salty area is expected to more than double.

Office of the Auditor General, Western Australia, Management of Salinity (2018)

9.7 · How Can Humans Repair and Sustain the Land?

Soil

Erosion
Soil erosion is soil loss when wind and water detach soil and carry it away. Weathering breaks rock down; erosion moves it.
Agriculture
Tillage exposes soil to wind and water erosion, and overgrazing strips its protective cover. Over-irrigation and excess chemicals degrade soil in other ways, through salt and contamination. Plow-based farming on Roman upland slopes ultimately reached bedrock.
9.7 · How Can Humans Repair and Sustain the Land?

Restoration

Sustainable Farming
Terracing, cover crops, hedgerows, crop rotation, and organic fertilizer reduce erosion and build fertility.
Grazing Management
Rotating livestock allows degraded soils to recover. Sustainable grazing maintains ground cover.
Mine Reclamation
Reclamation is site-specific: depending on the site, importing topsoil, planting trees, and sustainable grazing can rehabilitate mines. The Eden Project (Cornwall, England) turned a former clay pit into a major greenhouse and biome complex.

9.7 · Mining

Mining

  • Mining practices are not considered to be sustainable but abandoned mine sites can be reclaimed and rehabilitated to improve their ecological value.
  • Rehabilitative measures include importing topsoil, planting trees, and sustainable livestock grazing.
  • Globally, mines in Mongolia, the European Union, and China have been successfully rehabilitated.
Our World in Data, “Domestic material consumption per capita” (UN Environment Programme / SDG indicators): tonnes of biomass, fossil fuels, metal ores and other minerals used in each economy per person. It is counted where materials enter an economy, not as a full consumption footprint. Click a country, or switch to the line chart, to compare.

9.7 · Forestry and Urbanization

Forestry and Urbanization

Deforestation
Humans clear about 10.9 million hectares of forest per year (2015–2025, about the size of Tennessee); with regrowth, the net loss is about 4.1 million hectares a year (FAO, 2025). Deforestation can lead to land degradation. Deforestation is incredibly consequential and directly impacts all life-support systems.
Urbanization
Land-use change: converting forests into urban areas. Cities reclaim brownfields (contaminated industrial sites) for new use. San Antonio's River Walk restored a waterfront as a community amenity.
Flagstaff in the headlinesWhen the forest burns, the town floods

Show
Show
Year 1 of 30
About the model: a teaching simulation, not a forecast. Each company runs one copper deposit of 600 million tonnes of ore for up to 30 years. Ore grade, recovery, mining costs, water use and the cleanup bill are set in realistic proportion; the two real failures in the news are described as they happened. “Cash flow” is simplified: revenue minus operating costs, bond deposits and disasters, with no taxes, royalties or financing. Failure odds (about six times real-world rates, so a class sees what failures do), harm and safety multipliers are game assumptions. Podiums score every plan on the same standard site, so luck and class size do not decide them.
Sources and assumptions
Sources and assumptions
  • Mount Polley, 2014. Independent Expert Engineering Investigation and Review Panel (January 2015): the dam failed on August 4, 2014 through a glaciolacustrine clay layer in its foundation; at least 25 million m³ of tailings and water released. The panel recommended independent tailings review boards. Measured.
  • Brumadinho, 2019. Vale Córrego do Feijão Dam I, an upstream-raised dam inactive since 2016, failed January 25, 2019 by liquefaction (Robertson et al., Expert Panel report, December 2019); about 9.7 million m³ released, roughly 75% of the 11.7 to 12 million m³ stored; 270 people killed. Brazil’s National Mining Agency then ordered upstream dams decommissioned or converted. Measured.
  • Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management (ICMM, UNEP and PRI, August 2020). The game’s $150M buttress requirement for upstream dams is assumed.
  • Failure odds. Davies (2002), Geotechnical News: major tailings-dam failures about 1 in 700 to 1 in 1,750 per dam per year, roughly ten times water-retention dams. The game uses about 6× that rate, upstream ×2.6, downstream ×0.7, dry stack ×0.07 (relative values reflect the engineering consensus that upstream raising is least stable; sizes assumed).
  • Water. USGS Open-File Report 2012-1089: flotation concentrators withdraw about 0.96 m³ of water per tonne of ore. Well-run conventional ponds recover about 65 to 75% of process water (Cacciuttolo & Valenzuela, 2022, Water 14(11):1741, doi:10.3390/w14111741). Filtered tailings leave the plant as a cake of about 15% moisture (Hogg, 2010, Mine Waste 2010, Australian Centre for Geomechanics, Table 2), so most water is recovered at the plant. Game water per tonne: ponds 0.85 to 0.90, dry stack 0.25. Derived.
  • Ore and copper. Grades of 0.47 to 0.75% copper and 88% recovery are typical of porphyry copper mines (S&P Global; USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries). Copper prices of about $5,900 to $12,800 per tonne span real prices from 2015 to 2025. Derived.
  • Costs, cleanup bills, jobs and towns. Mining costs of about $21 to $27 per tonne of ore, the per-hectare cleanup costs, water treatment in perpetuity, jobs of about 400 + 75 per million tonnes mined, and town growth are assumed teaching values in plausible proportion.
  • Reclamation bonds. As in U.S. and Canadian financial-assurance rules, the bond is sized to the estimated cleanup liability (here a chosen 0 to 100% of it), topped up as the mine grows, and released at successful closure; an under-bonded closure leaves the shortfall to the public. Cleanup costs per hectare are assumed.
  • Facilities. After a wet-dam failure the failed facility is closed as it stands and new tailings go to a new downstream-raised facility; each keeps its own area, cleanup cost and drainage. Assumed.
  • Scores. Land & safety and the podiums use only each company’s own mine. Podiums rerun every plan on one standard site (monsoon climate, solid bedrock, average ore, a town 12 km downstream) with dam failure counted as odds times a typical cost. Game method.
  • River. Each mine adds acid drainage and any spill to a shared river; the river recovers 18% of the load between mines. A stylized model, assumed.
Chapter 9 · Key Concepts

Land: How Does It Shape Us?

Rock Cycle
Igneous → weathering/erosion → sedimentary → metamorphic → back to igneous
Rare Earth Elements
Critical for clean tech; extraction carries environmental justice costs
Delta
A landform formed by the deposition of sediments at a river's mouth
Soil Horizons (O,A,B,C)
Layered soil profile from organic topsoil to parent rock
CLORPT
Climate, Organisms, Relief, Parent material, Time: the drivers of soil formation
Healthy Soil
Supports plant growth and nutrient cycling, the base of sustainable land use
Soil Erosion
Soil loss when wind and water detach soil and carry it away
Land Degradation
Loss of the land's productivity; deforestation is a leading cause
Land-Use Change
Converting land from one use to another, such as forests into urban areas
Glomalin
Humus protein discovered 1996 that binds soil particles together
Tillage & Erosion
Plowing exposes soil; terracing and cover crops prevent loss
Mine Reclamation
Topsoil, trees and managed grazing return a mined site to use
